DETAILS
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. [Correct Reference Solution] MAJOR -- Core domain and business logic
   Reading a newline-terminated file after a binary buffer with an unterminated final line
   incorrectly transfers the old line's missing-newline flag to the newly read final line.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: Start with command-line file `original` containing the bytes `a\x00`; supply piped
     stdin `r addition\nw result\nQ\n`, where `addition` contains `b\n`. The binary line
     originally lacks a newline, so reading `addition` at the end inserts a separator before
     `b`; because `b` arrives terminated, the resulting buffer must write `a\x00\nb\n`. In the
     reference, `was_bare` is true and `inserted` clears the original tail's flag at lines
     691-695. The read then creates the `b` line with `no_newline=False` at lines 698-714, but
     lines 722-723 set that new last line's flag to true merely because `was_bare` was true.
     Flip: `write_file` lines 744-749 consequently writes `a\x00\nb`, omitting the final newline
     required for the newly read line.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed.txt:760-767, environment/app/docs/ed.txt:942-947,
     environment/app/docs/ed-errata.txt:79-84, solution/pyed/ed.py:689-723,
     solution/pyed/ed.py:740-749

2. [Correct Reference Solution] MAJOR -- Core domain and business logic
   Reading a newline-terminated file after a binary buffer with an unterminated last line
   incorrectly removes the newline from the newly appended last line.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: Put the three bytes `a\0b` in `original`, the two bytes `c\n` in `second`, and run
     with piped stdin containing `r second\nw output\nQ\n` and FILE `original`. The original
     bare line needs a separating newline when another line is appended; `second` already
     terminates its own line. The contract therefore requires `output` to contain `a\0b\nc\n` (6
     bytes), with a write count of 6. The reference detects `was_bare`, clears the original
     marker at lines 691–695, and reads `c\n` with `no_newline=False` at lines 698–714. But
     lines 720–723 then set the new last line's marker to True solely because `was_bare` was
     True. Flip: `write_file` consequently emits `a\0b\nc` (5 bytes) and prints a write count of
     5.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed-errata.txt:79-84, environment/app/docs/ed.txt:942-947,
     solution/pyed/ed.py:689-723, solution/pyed/ed.py:740-754

3. [Correct Reference Solution] MAJOR
   A backslash-continued global list stops consuming input at its empty continuation line, so a
   following q executes after all selected lines instead of as part of the list.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: Start with an existing two-line file containing `x\ny\n` and supply `g/./\\\n\nq\n`
     on standard input. The errata explicitly says the empty segment prints each selected line
     twice and the following q belongs to the list. Thus q stops list execution during the first
     selected line: the expected printed lines are `x\nx\n`. The reference assembles only the
     first two script lines into the list, printing `x\nx\ny\ny\n`, then reads q as a top-level
     command. Flip: stdout has two extra `y` lines, contrary to the required byte-for-byte
     comparison.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed-errata.txt:67-71, solution/pyed/ed.py:137-159,
     solution/pyed/ed.py:1346-1385

4. [Correct Reference Solution] MAJOR -- core domain and business logic
   Valid long bounded-repeat regular expressions are parsed but matched by unbounded Python
   recursion, causing an unhandled RecursionError instead of GNU ed's successful substitution.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: run with stdin as a pipe containing `a\n` followed by exactly 2,000 ASCII `a` bytes
     and `\n.\ns/a\\{2000\\}/X/\nw out\nq\n`. This is one ASCII text line and uses BRE bounded
     repetition, which the manual defines. The parser accepts the interval (`lo=hi=2000`), then
     `s` calls `rx.search`; the repetition loop recursively invokes itself for each matched `a`,
     exceeding Python's normal recursion limit before a match result is returned. The exception
     is not caught by command execution. Flip: GNU ed 1.19 accepts this repeat count, replaces
     the 2,000-character line with `X`, writes `out` containing exactly `X\n`, emits `2\n` for
     `w out`, and exits zero. The reference emits no such byte count, does not create `out`, and
     exits nonzero from the unhandled exception.
   Where to look: instruction.md:1-10, environment/app/docs/ed.txt:527-536,
     environment/app/docs/ed.txt:870-902, solution/pyed/ed.py:632-656,
     solution/pyed/posixre.py:88-124, solution/pyed/posixre.py:305-317 (+1 more)

5. [Correct Reference Solution] MAJOR -- core domain and business logic
   The append command accepts a reversed two-address range, although only '=' may accept one
   under the GNU ed 1.19 erratum.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: with piped stdin, start an empty editor and supply `a\none\ntwo\n.\n2,1a\nX\n.\nw
     out\nQ\n`. The initial append creates lines 1 and 2. extract_addresses parses `2,1` as
     first_addr=2 and second_addr=1. exec_command's `a` branch calls append_lines with
     second_addr=1 without check_addr_range, so `X` is inserted after line 1 and `w out` writes
     `one\nX\ntwo\n` (10 bytes). Contract/GNU behavior: erratum 3 permits the reversed pair only
     for `=`; `2,1a` must fail with `?\n`, must not enter input mode, and must not insert X.
     Flip: both stdout and the required resulting out file differ; a correct implementation
     rejects before consuming X as append input.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed-errata.txt:19-20, environment/app/docs/ed.txt:345-347,
     solution/pyed/ed.py:1124-1131, solution/pyed/ed.py:1329-1333

6. [Correct Reference Solution] MAJOR -- core domain and business logic
   The append command clears the undo stack before determining whether input mode inserts any
   line, so a successful empty append wrongly destroys the prior undoable buffer modification.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: with stdin a pipe, run `a\nfoo\n.\na\n.\nu\n=\nQ\n`. The first append inserts `foo`
     and records UADD. The second append is terminated immediately by `.`; per the append
     contract it enters no text and leaves current at the addressed line, so it modifies no
     buffer. Nevertheless exec_command calls clear_undo_stack before append_lines; append_lines
     returns at `.` without push_undo. Thus u sees an empty ustack, emits `?`, and `=` prints
     `1`. Flip: a conforming implementation retains the first append as the last
     buffer-modifying command; u removes `foo` and `=` prints `0`. This is a contract-valid
     script and changes both stdout and buffer state.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed.txt:608-613, environment/app/docs/ed.txt:780-785,
     solution/pyed/ed.py:231-256, solution/pyed/ed.py:369-373, solution/pyed/ed.py:1124-1130

7. [Correct Reference Solution] MAJOR -- input validation and contract-bound behavior
   The substitution parser accepts a repeat-form suffix character such as g as an explicit
   substitution delimiter, although the contract excludes characters used by the alternate
   repeat-substitution syntax.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: run with piped stdin `a\nx\n.\nsgxgyg\np\nQ\n`. `s` is parsed at
     solution/pyed/ed.py:1086; get_pattern_for_s takes the first `g` as delimiter, extracts
     pattern `x`, extract_replacement takes `y`, and the closing `g` is accepted. The reference
     therefore changes line 1 from `x` to `y`; `p` emits `y\n`, and Q exits 0. Flip: under the
     contract's delimiter exclusion, the same `sgxgyg` command is invalid, so ed emits `?\n`,
     leaves the line as `x`, the following p emits `x\n`, and the non-loose piped session has
     nonzero status. A plausible implementation that copies this parser behavior passes all
     ordinary-delimiter cases but fails this contract-defined malformed-command boundary.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed.txt:904-910, solution/pyed/ed.py:480-497,
     solution/pyed/ed.py:1086-1114, solution/pyed/ed.py:1411-1420

8. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR -- missing behavioral coverage
   Fixture construction cannot create an existing subdirectory, so the verifier cannot
   distinguish an ed implementation that rejects otherwise valid file-command paths beneath one.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: In a workdir with an existing directory `sub`, run with pipe stdin `a\nX\n.\nw
     sub/x\nQ\n`. The in-scope `w` command must write `sub/x` containing `X\n`; rejecting the
     path instead emits `?\n` and does not write it. Flip: An implementation that handles the
     tested flat filenames but refuses file arguments beneath directories would fail this
     contract-legal run. It clears the graded path condition because `workdir()` only opens each
     fixture filename directly and never creates directories; even the visible `w sub/x.txt`
     case in `options.jsonl:8` has no `sub` directory and expects failure. The comparison at
     145-147 therefore has no successful nested-path case to distinguish the implementations.
     `snapshot()` also records a directory only as `None`, not its contents.
   Where to look: tests/test_outputs.py:86-105, tests/test_outputs.py:140-155,
     tests/cases/options.jsonl:8, environment/app/docs/ed.txt:795-800

9. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR -- missing behavioral coverage
   No shown case checks that '&' repeats an entire multiline G or V command list rather than
   just its first command.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: With an empty initial buffer and piped script
     `a\na\na\n.\nG/a/\ns/a/A/\\\np\n&\nQ\n`, the first selected line receives the two-command
     list `s/a/A/` then `p`; '&' must repeat both commands for the second selected line. Flip:
     An implementation that stores only the first command for '&' omits the second `p` on that
     line, changing stdout. It can still implement the shown '&' cases, whose repeated lists are
     single-command lists, and the shown multiline-list case, which does not use '&'. The byte
     comparison at tests/test_outputs.py:147 would reject it if this combined case were
     supplied, but none of tests/cases/interactive_global.jsonl:1-14 supplies it. The three NOT
     SHOWN mixed-script files could not be inspected.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed.txt:668-690,
     tests/cases/interactive_global.jsonl:1-14, tests/test_outputs.py:140-155

10. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR -- missing behavioral coverage
   The shown cases do not reject an `f` filename attached directly to its command letter,
   although the contract requires separating filenames with whitespace.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: With no initial file and pipe input `fout\nQ\n`, GNU ed treats `fout` as an invalid
     command and prints `?`. Flip: An otherwise-correct implementation whose `f` handler accepts
     `line[1:]` as its filename prints `out` instead. It clears the shown `f target`, `f
     other.txt` and bare-`f` cases, while the attached-filename rejection cases shown are for
     `e` and `w`, not `f`. The unshown mixed_scripts_6–8 cannot be assessed here.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed.txt:597-599, tests/cases/files_and_write.jsonl:47-54,
     tests/test_outputs.py:140-155

11. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR -- missing behavioral coverage
   The shown focused substitutions do not distinguish setting current address to the last
   substituted line from setting it to the last addressed line.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: With empty initial buffer, use `a\nax\nb\n.\n1,2s/a/A/\n.=\nQ\n`. Only line 1
     changes, so GNU ed prints `1` for `.=`, whereas an implementation that always selects the
     range endpoint prints `2`. Flip: That ordinary shortcut clears the shown
     ranged-substitution cases that subsequently print an entire range; the explicit `.= ` split
     case checks a different branch. No assertion in the shown focused substitution and error
     cases distinguishes these addresses. The unshown mixed-script files prevent a claim about
     their contents.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed.txt:897-901, tests/cases/substitute.jsonl:1-14,
     tests/cases/substitute.jsonl:33-34

12. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR -- missing behavioral coverage
   The shown cases exercise several substitution delimiters but do not enforce acceptance of
   every legal delimiter.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: `a\na\n.\ns~a~b~p\nQ\n` is contract-legal and should print `b\n`. Flip: A plausible
     parser accepting `/`, `|`, `#`, `@` and `:` but rejecting `~` matches the shown focused
     delimiter cases yet prints `?\n` here. The missing-final-delimiter cases check another
     branch, not acceptance of `~`. The three unshown mixed-script files cannot be credited as
     checks.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed.txt:904-910, tests/cases/substitute.jsonl:36-41,
     tests/cases/substitute.jsonl:53-58, tests/cases/global_commands.jsonl:35

13. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR -- missing behavioral coverage
   The shown replacement tests check selected escapes, but not the rule that backslash also
   quotes an ordinary character.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: `a\na\n.\ns/a/\q/p\nQ\n` must print `q\n`: the backslash removes any special meaning
     of the following `q`. Flip: A plausible replacement parser that recognizes only
     backreferences, escaped delimiters, `\&`, `\%`, `\\` and escaped newline would retain `\q`
     or reject it, while clearing the shown focused escape cases. No shown focused assertion
     uses an ordinary quoted replacement character; mixed_scripts_6–8 were not shown.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed.txt:919-921, tests/cases/substitute.jsonl:26-27,
     tests/cases/substitute.jsonl:40-43, tests/cases/substitute.jsonl:60

14. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR -- missing behavioral coverage
   The visible global-command cases do not enforce the rule that encountering u stops execution
   of that global command list after its first selected line.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: With the two-line `a\na\n` fixture f_45, use `g/a/s/a/A/p\\\nu\n,p\nQ\n`. A global
     implementation that ordinarily iterates every initially selected line but forgets the
     special u stop is a plausible genuine attempt. Flip: after printing the first substituted
     `A` and executing u, such an implementation continues to the second selected line and
     prints another `A`; GNU ed executes the list only once. The focused visible global-command
     cases contain no u in a command list, so their byte-exact comparisons do not distinguish
     these implementations. Coverage in the files marked NOT SHOWN remains unverified.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed.txt:968-969, tests/cases/global_commands.jsonl:30-45,
     tests/cases/fixtures.json:356-360, tests/test_outputs.py:140-155

15. [Correct Reference Solution] MINOR -- input validation and contract-bound behavior
   The reference never enforces GNU ed's documented maximum line length or maximum number of
   lines, instead storing lines and counts in unbounded Python objects.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: a file consisting of 2,147,483,647 ASCII bytes followed by a newline has a line one
     byte beyond the documented INT_MAX - 1 maximum; similarly, a file with 2,147,483,647
     one-byte newline-terminated lines is one line beyond INT_MAX - 2. In read_file, each input
     line reaches put_sbuf_line (697-714), which creates Line(text[:j]) (195-200), with no
     size/count check. Flip: GNU's stated buffer limits do not permit these inputs, while this
     implementation attempts to accept and represent them (or dies from host allocation rather
     than producing GNU ed's bounded behavior). The construction is maximally adversarial and
     outside ordinary few-dozen-line scripts, hence Minor.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed.txt:949-953, solution/pyed/ed.py:189-200,
     solution/pyed/ed.py:697-714

16. [Sound Verifier] MINOR -- missing behavioral coverage
   The visible extended-regex cases do not make literal matching by escaped `\|` decisive.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: A contract-legal distinguishing run uses `-E` and pipe script
     `a\nx|y\n.\n1s/x\\|y/Z/p\nQ\n`. GNU ed treats `\|` literally and prints `Z\n`; an
     implementation that incorrectly retains basic-regex alternation would replace only `x` and
     print `Z|y\n`. Flip: The resulting byte-output assertion would differ. The 12 shown
     `regex_extended` cases exercise unescaped `|`, not this match. Some visible mixed scripts
     contain `\|` under `-E`, but their shared `f_other_03` fixture has no pipe character. The
     contents of mixed_scripts_6–8 are NOT SHOWN, so reachability across the entire corpus is
     unverified; this is an advisory finding, not proof that the wrong implementation clears
     every case.
   Where to look: instruction.md:7, tests/cases/regex_extended.jsonl:1-12,
     tests/cases/fixtures.json:512-520

17. [Sound Verifier] MINOR -- missing behavioral coverage
   No shown case makes a one-address join's clearing of an existing undo stack decisive.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: a contract-legal script on an initially empty buffer,
     `a\nx\n.\n1s/x/y/\n1j\nu\n,p\nQ\n`, distinguishes the rule: `1j` leaves `y` unchanged but
     clears undo, so `u` must fail. Flip: an implementation that treats the no-op join as
     leaving undo intact would restore `x`; it could satisfy the shown standalone join cases.
     Whether it passes every graded case is unverified: tests/cases/undo.jsonl and
     mixed_scripts_6–8 were NOT SHOWN.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed-errata.txt:55-56,
     tests/cases/delete_join_move_copy.jsonl:17-18, tests/cases/roster.json:10-17

18. [Sound Verifier] MINOR -- missing behavioral coverage
   No shown case checks that a global command selecting zero lines clears a preceding undo
   stack.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: `a\nx\n.\n1s/x/y/\ng/nomatch/p\nu\n,p\nQ\n` is a cheap distinguishing script. Flip:
     GNU ed's zero-selection global clears undo, making `u` fail and leaving `y`; an
     implementation that returns early without clearing undo restores `x`. The shown no-match
     global cases do not subsequently make undo decisive. A whole-suite pass is unverified
     because tests/cases/undo.jsonl and mixed_scripts_6–8 were NOT SHOWN.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed-errata.txt:58-59,
     tests/cases/global_commands.jsonl:10-11, tests/cases/roster.json:10-17

19. [Sound Verifier] MINOR -- overstrict comparator
   The package audit mistakes an executable-format magic prefix in inert data for a delivered
   executable program, falsely rejecting a contract-legal submission.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: A complete pure-Python ed implementation can keep a lookup table at
     /app/pyed/table.dat whose bytes begin b'\x7fELF' but do not constitute an executable, and
     read it only as data. Neither reading that table nor retaining it starts a program or loads
     native code. Flip: test_delivered_package_is_standard_library_python calls audit_package on
     every delivered file; raw.startswith(EXECUTABLE_MAGIC) raises AssertionError for table.dat
     before its otherwise-correct behavior can be graded. This requires an unusual data header
     rather than an ordinary implementation choice, so the false reject is Minor.
   Where to look: instruction.md:10, tests/test_outputs.py:207-221,
     tests/test_outputs.py:248-249

20. [Sound Verifier] MINOR -- missing behavioral coverage
   The shown one-address j cases do not distinguish an implementation that leaves undo history
   intact.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: After an edit, a contract-legal `1j` on a one-line buffer followed by `u`
     distinguishes the rule: GNU ed clears the history, so u fails, whereas an implementation
     treating j as a no-op without clearing history undoes the edit. Flip: The shown one-address
     j scripts at delete_join_move_copy.jsonl:17,30 never issue u afterward. Whether this
     implementation passes every graded input is unverified because tests/cases/undo.jsonl and
     mixed_scripts_6–8.jsonl were not shown; this is advisory rather than a confirmed
     corpus-wide bypass.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed-errata.txt:55-56,
     tests/cases/delete_join_move_copy.jsonl:17, tests/cases/delete_join_move_copy.jsonl:30

   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed.txt:709-714, tests/cases/fixtures.json:158-162,
     tests/cases/delete_join_move_copy.jsonl:17, tests/cases/delete_join_move_copy.jsonl:30

24. [Sound Verifier] MINOR
   No shown V case applies an explicit address range, permitting an implementation that ignores
   V's range while handling its default range correctly.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: With lines a and b, run 1,1V/b/ and supply p as the interactive command list. Flip:

typos.explanation: No typos were found in filenames, paths, commands, or variable names across instruction.md, task.toml, Dockerfiles, guard.py, ed.py, or posixre.py. agentic.explanation: The agent has no network access at solve time and the agent image deliberately omits `ed`, so there is no oracle to diff against locally; the agent must iteratively write, test, and debug a large multi-file implementation purely from the manual and errata text, which cannot be done in a single zero-shot generation.

difficult.explanation: Requires reconstructing a stateful C-derived editor (address arithmetic, undo/redo of add-delete-move records, mark lifetime, global command active-lists, interactive G/V) and a from-scratch POSIX leftmost-longest regex engine (Python's `re` cannot do this), while reasoning about numerous documented behavioral quirks (ed-errata.txt) that diverge from the manual. interesting.explanation: Reimplementing standard Unix tools in pure Python for minimal/scratch container images (busybox/toybox-style) is a genuine real-world need for people maintaining legacy `ed`/`sed` scripts in stripped-down environments; the task's own framing ('minimal images have no ed... maintenance scripts... piped into it') describes a plausible professional scenario.

binary_reward.explanation: test.sh only ever writes the literal string '0' or '1' to /logs/verifier/reward.txt (initial 0, then 1 iff pytest's exit code is 0, else 0 again). No fractional, weighted, or clamped score is ever written.

✅ pass - verifiable: tests/test.sh runs `python3 -I -m pytest ... /tests/test_outputs.py` which for every one of 1816 committed cases (roster.json cross-checked against the jsonl files at collection time) executes the image's own /usr/bin/ed to derive the expected result and the candidate through guard.py, comparing stdout byte-for-byte, zero/non-zero exit status, and the final directory snapshot. No network installs occur in test.sh (pytest/ctrf/ed are baked into tests/Dockerfile). The comparison is deterministic given LC_ALL=C and fixed inputs, and no LLM-as-judge is used.
✅ pass - solvable: solution/pyed/ed.py (~1500 lines) and posixre.py (~360 lines) provide a structurally complete port of GNU ed's algorithm (line-node list, undo stack, active-list globals, POSIX leftmost-longest backtracking matcher) that solve.sh copies into /app/pyed, matching every family described in the instruction and errata. expert_time_estimate_hours=12 is on the high side of 'a few hours' but the task explicitly frames this as a mechanical, spec-driven port for someone who already knows GNU ed's algorithm, which is consistent with the size of the reference implementation.
✅ pass - difficult: Requires reconstructing a stateful C-derived editor (address arithmetic, undo/redo of add-delete-move records, mark lifetime, global command active-lists, interactive G/V) and a from-scratch POSIX leftmost-longest regex engine (Python's `re` cannot do this), while reasoning about numerous documented behavioral quirks (ed-errata.txt) that diverge from the manual. This goes well beyond a standard course project and would challenge an experienced systems engineer.
✅ pass - interesting: Reimplementing standard Unix tools in pure Python for minimal/scratch container images (busybox/toybox-style) is a genuine real-world need for people maintaining legacy `ed`/`sed` scripts in stripped-down environments; the task's own framing ('minimal images have no ed... maintenance scripts... piped into it') describes a plausible professional scenario.
✅ pass - outcome_verified: Grading is purely behavioral: byte-identical stdout, exit status, and final file contents versus a live GNU ed 1.19 run. The stdlib-only / no-subprocess / no-native-code constraints are part of the domain requirement itself (the whole point is a portable pure-Python replacement) rather than an arbitrary 'use this tool' instruction, and they are enforced only as anti-cheat via guard.py, not by inspecting the agent's implementation approach otherwise.
✅ pass - anti_cheat_robustness: The real /usr/bin/ed is chmod 700 (root-only) before any candidate code runs, so the candidate cannot read or exec it; guard.py's audit hook and meta-path Warden block subprocess/exec/fork/ctypes calls and any import origin outside stdlib+delivered files, and test_delivered_package_is_standard_library_python() additionally scans delivered bytes for ELF/PE/Mach-O magic to catch a smuggled native binary. Five guardcheck probes plus a synthetic-package audit test validate the launcher's own effectiveness. Ground truth is produced live in the verifier container from the actual ed binary, never exposed to the agent.
✅ pass - task_security: No exfiltration, obfuscation, or destructive commands were found in any Dockerfile, script, or test case. A couple of generated test scripts read /etc/hostname to exercise the `-r` restricted-mode denial path, but this reads only non-sensitive local data inside the verifier's own sandbox and never transmits it anywhere; it is a legitimate feature test, not exfiltration.
✅ pass - functional_verification: Verification is entirely execution-based: it runs both the reference `ed` and the candidate binary on the same script/files and diffs actual stdout, exit code, and resulting files. No test relies on grepping the candidate's source for keywords (the only source inspection, audit_package, checks import provenance and binary magic bytes for anti-cheat, not correctness of behavior).
✅ pass - deterministic_reproducible: Both Dockerfiles pin the exact same base image by sha256 digest; pytest and pytest-json-ctrf are pinned exact versions in tests/Dockerfile; the apt-installed `ed` package is intentionally unpinned per accepted apt convention. LC_ALL=C, fixed env dict, and no external network calls are used at verify time, so repeated runs against the same candidate should be stable.
✅ pass - essential_difficulty: The hard parts are genuine algorithmic/semantic issues (current-address tracking, undo-of-undo, POSIX leftmost-longest matching, global active-list semantics) rather than arbitrary formatting; the byte-level output conventions being matched (e.g. escaping in `l`, newline-count reporting) are themselves core, well-specified parts of ed's behavior described in the manual/errata, not incidental clerical detail.
✅ pass - test_instruction_alignment: Every checked property (stdout equality, exit-status equality, file-state equality, stdlib-only/no-subprocess/no-native-code enforcement) is explicitly stated in instruction.md. The extra guard self-tests (test_launcher_stops_delegation_and_foreign_code, test_the_package_audit_takes_data_and_refuses_programs) validate the verifier's own enforcement machinery rather than adding new requirements on the candidate.
✅ pass - novel: While GNU ed's C source is public and could inform training data, faithfully reproducing its exact byte-level behavior including the author-verified errata list, and building a from-scratch POSIX leftmost-longest regex engine, requires substantial engineering and cannot be trivially reproduced by memorized snippets alone, especially with 1816 unseen generated test scripts as the actual grading corpus.
✅ pass - agentic: The agent has no network access at solve time and the agent image deliberately omits `ed`, so there is no oracle to diff against locally; the agent must iteratively write, test, and debug a large multi-file implementation purely from the manual and errata text, which cannot be done in a single zero-shot generation.
✅ pass - reviewable: Ground truth is never hardcoded: the verifier runs the real GNU ed 1.19 at test time and diffs against it, so a non-specialist reviewer can trust the actual reference tool rather than an author's assertions. The errata file explicitly documents that every quirk 'was checked against the program itself,' further aiding review.
✅ pass - instruction_concision: instruction.md is a dense but non-repetitive paragraph-style description using absolute paths (`/app/pyed/ed.py`, `/app/docs/ed.txt`) and backticks for options/commands, states the end goal and exclusions up front, and does not prescribe an implementation approach. Its length is proportional to the genuine scope constraints (coverage exceptions, byte-for-byte comparison rule, stdlib-only rule) rather than filler.
✅ pass - solution_quality: solve.sh performs a real file copy of a working, non-trivial implementation (not an echoed answer); the large files (ed.py, posixre.py) are kept as separate files under solution/ rather than inlined as heredocs, matching the guidance for files longer than ~20 lines.
✅ pass - separate_verifier_configured: All verifier reads are confined to the declared artifact (/app) and files baked into tests/Dockerfile (cases, guard.py, guardcheck, guardvendor, copied to /opt/pyedguard). Verifier tooling (pytest, pytest-json-ctrf, `ed`) is installed at image-build time, not in test.sh. The same base image digest is pinned identically in environment/Dockerfile and tests/Dockerfile, and there are no duplicated shared assets that could drift.
✅ pass - environment_hygiene: environment/Dockerfile only COPYs app/ and installs generic scaffolding packages (tmux, asciinema, patch, ca-certificates), not test/solution deps; .dockerignore additionally excludes tests/ and solution/. tests/Dockerfile owns all test-only dependencies (pytest, ctrf, ed) baked at build time. Both Dockerfiles follow apt-get update + install + rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* and leave apt packages unpinned as expected, while pip packages are version-pinned.
✅ pass - structured_data_schema: The expected 'structured' output is GNU ed's own well-defined textual protocol (print/list/number formats, byte counts, prompts, `?` diagnostics), which is normatively documented in /app/docs/ed.txt and /app/docs/ed-errata.txt, both explicitly referenced by instruction.md as the authoritative spec.
✅ pass - typos: No typos were found in filenames, paths, commands, or variable names across instruction.md, task.toml, Dockerfiles, guard.py, ed.py, or posixre.py. The lone unusual spelling ('occurences') appears inside the verbatim reproduced GNU ed manual text (environment/app/docs/ed.txt), which is third-party reference material rather than task-authored content.
✅ pass - difficulty_explanation_quality: difficulty_explanation enumerates concrete sources of difficulty (address forms, current-address tracking, undo-of-undo, global active-list semantics, interactive G/V, POSIX leftmost-longest matching that Python's `re` lacks, error/exit-status handling) and explicitly states the test corpus is synthetically generated from the task's own grammar with no external corpus, addressing the data-provenance requirement. The 'who does this in real life' angle is covered in the adjacent relevant_experience field rather than restated inline, but the substantive difficulty analysis is thorough and non-vague.
✅ pass - solution_explanation_quality: solution_explanation accurately summarizes the two-file approach (posixre.py's exhaustive leftmost/longest backtracking matcher; ed.py's circular line-node list with an undo stack of add/delete/move records) and this description is fully consistent with what solution/pyed/ed.py and posixre.py actually implement.
✅ pass - verification_explanation_quality: verification_explanation accurately describes the roster/fixture cross-check, per-case comparison of stdout/exit-status/files against a live GNU ed run, the root-only permissions on the reference binary, the unprivileged launcher and its five probe checks, and the package audit — all of which match what guard.py and test_outputs.py actually do. No inequality-based tolerances are used, so no calibration justification is required.
✅ pass - category_and_tags: category=Software is correct for a command-line tool reimplementation. subcategory=Languages is a defensible fit given the task centers on implementing a command grammar and a POSIX regular-expression engine (a language-processing task), though 'Systems'/'Command-line tools' could also be argued as an alternative fit. Tags (gnu-ed, line-editor, posix-regex, undo, reimplementation) are specific and directly descriptive of the task's skills.
✅ pass - no_extraneous_files: Every file traced back to a use: environment/app/* is copied into the agent image and referenced by instruction.md; tests/cases/* are loaded and roster-checked by test_outputs.py; tests/guardcheck/* and tests/guardvendor/thirdparty.py are exercised by test_launcher_stops_delegation_and_foreign_code; solution/pyed/* is copied by solve.sh. No cruft, backups, or unused assets were found.
✅ pass - verifier_execution_isolation: Candidate code is always invoked via `setpriv --reuid=65534 --regid=65534 --clear-groups --no-new-privs` inside guard.py, never imported into the root pytest process. /tests and /logs/verifier are chmod 700 and the real `ed` binary is made root-only before any candidate code runs, and test.sh derives the reward from pytest's root-observed exit code, not anything the candidate can touch. One minor weakness: run() captures stdout via subprocess.PIPE and calls a second, untimed `proc.communicate()` after a timeout-triggered killpg, which could hang if a candidate double-forks a detached daemon holding the pipe open — but since reward.txt defaults to 0 and is only set to 1 on a clean pytest success, this could at most cause a timeout/fail, not a forged pass.
✅ pass - ctrf_reporting: test.sh runs pytest with `--ctrf /logs/verifier/ctrf.json` against test_outputs.py, which defines one named test per manual area/bucket plus the guard self-checks, giving genuine per-test CTRF granularity.
➖ not_applicable - do_not_modify_enforced: instruction.md contains no 'do not modify / must remain unchanged' constraint on any concrete artifact (file, config, schema, etc.); its constraints are behavioral (no subprocess, no native code, stdlib only), which are covered under anti_cheat_robustness/outcome_verified instead.
✅ pass - binary_reward: test.sh only ever writes the literal string '0' or '1' to /logs/verifier/reward.txt (initial 0, then 1 iff pytest's exit code is 0, else 0 again). No fractional, weighted, or clamped score is ever written.

[correct_reference_solution] Major
  [part 1 of 11] The reference installs a pure-Python editor and implements the listed option, address, and regex distinctions. One reachable boundary between two ordinary file commands breaks the byte-for-byte contract: after r appends a newline-terminated file to a binary buffer whose former last line lacked a newline, the reference incorrectly marks the newly read last line as unterminated. A subsequent w therefore produces different file bytes and a different stdout byte count. The same mechanism accounts for the affected broad guarantees and command-coverage rows.

  [part 2 of 11] The interactive-list, error, EOF, invocation, mark, range, and leading-repeat paths have corresponding implementations. A reachable binary-file transition is wrong: after inserting a newline before data read by r, the reference marks the newly read, newline-terminated final line as lacking a newline. A subsequent write therefore changes the required file bytes. The same defect affects the overlapping command, binary-input, and erratum obligations.

  [part 3 of 11] The reference follows the specified regex, command-list, undo, filename, and write-warning branches in this checklist. Its binary-file read path nevertheless transfers a missing-final-newline marker to a newly appended line that arrived with a newline. A subsequent write loses that newline and reports the wrong byte count.

  [part 4 of 11] The reference handles the listed invocation, input-mode, prompting and semicolon-search transitions, but two contract-valid boundary cases diverge. Its binary-file read path transfers a missing-newline state to a newly read line even when that line arrived with a newline. Separately, its comment-command path skips the range check that rejects reversed ranges for commands other than =. Each changes observable output or file contents.

  [part 5 of 11] I traced the listed address boundaries through the parser, including omitted endpoints, a three-address range, cumulative offsets that temporarily leave the buffer, search wraparound, and unset marks in empty versus nonempty buffers. I also checked empty-pattern reuse, the compilation-time `I` restriction, and the BRE literal paths. No contract-valid counterexample was established for this checklist part.

  [part 6 of 11] The reference implements the listed regex syntax and command parsing, but its exhaustive matcher recursively expands repetitions. A modestly long, otherwise valid line makes a basic `*` substitution terminate with an uncaught recursion error instead of producing GNU ed's output. This affects both the general basic-regexp obligation and its specific repetition obligation.

  [part 7 of 11] The append, change, delete, edit, and ordinary global-selection paths follow the cited contract rules at their relevant empty-buffer, end-of-buffer, and error transitions. The documented GNU 1.19 exception for a backslash-continued global list followed by an empty line is not reproduced: the reference treats the subsequent q as a top-level command. With more than one selected line, that changes byte-for-byte output.

  [part 8 of 11] No contract-valid counterexample was established for these obligations. In particular, a one-line join clears undo without replacing its line; a move destination equal to the range's last address passes the strict-interior rejection; and an empty interactive global list leaves the selected line current without executing a command. For an ordinary global list, a bare newline instead reaches the null-command printing path. The reference also distinguishes a modified-buffer q warning from unconditional Q. This is a static audit of the shown reference, not a claim based on running GNU ed.

  [part 9 of 11] The ordinary address, copy, write, cut-buffer, scroll, and quit paths are implemented. Undo has a contract-visible binary-file counterexample: r changes an existing line's missing-newline state, but the undo records only line-link operations and cannot restore that state. The same defect applies when r is executed within a global command.

  [part 10 of 11] The command branches cover the ordinary z, comment, number, null, and substitution cases. A boundary between match counting and zero-length matching is wrong: for a positive COUNT, the reference re-searches the unchanged suffix after an empty match and counts that same occurrence again. The manual explicitly permits an empty leftmost match and defines COUNT as selecting the COUNTth match; the erratum about refusing repeated empty matches applies to g, not this count form.

  [part 11 of 11] I found no constructible, contract-valid divergence for these obligations. For example, an escaped newline is retained in the replacement, then split when the replacement is inserted; a search updates the regexp subsequently selected by abbreviated sr; and undo inside a global list clears the list of remaining selected lines. The documented INT_MAX limits could not be adjudicated with a cheap input in the stated runtime and memory environment.

  Findings (3):
    1. (Major) [1 - Core domain and business logic] Reading a newline-terminated file after a binary buffer with an unterminated final line incorrectly transfers the old line's missing-newline flag to the newly read final line.
       Reach: Start with command-line file `original` containing the bytes `a\x00`; supply piped stdin `r addition\nw result\nQ\n`, where `addition` contains `b\n`. The binary line originally lacks a newline, so reading `addition` at the end inserts a separator before `b`; because `b` arrives terminated, the resulting buffer must write `a\x00\nb\n`. In the reference, `was_bare` is true and `inserted` clears the original tail's flag at lines 691-695. The read then creates the `b` line with `no_newline=False` at lines 698-714, but lines 722-723 set that new last line's flag to true merely because `was_bare` was true. Flip: `write_file` lines 744-749 consequently writes `a\x00\nb`, omitting the final newline required for the newly read line.
       Cited: environment/app/docs/ed.txt:760-767, environment/app/docs/ed.txt:942-947, environment/app/docs/ed-errata.txt:79-84, solution/pyed/ed.py:689-723, solution/pyed/ed.py:740-749
    2. (Major) [1 - Core domain and business logic] Reading a newline-terminated file after a binary buffer with an unterminated last line incorrectly removes the newline from the newly appended last line.
       Reach: Put the three bytes `a\0b` in `original`, the two bytes `c\n` in `second`, and run with piped stdin containing `r second\nw output\nQ\n` and FILE `original`. The original bare line needs a separating newline when another line is appended; `second` already terminates its own line. The contract therefore requires `output` to contain `a\0b\nc\n` (6 bytes), with a write count of 6. The reference detects `was_bare`, clears the original marker at lines 691–695, and reads `c\n` with `no_newline=False` at lines 698–714. But lines 720–723 then set the new last line's marker to True solely because `was_bare` was True. Flip: `write_file` consequently emits `a\0b\nc` (5 bytes) and prints a write count of 5.
       Cited: environment/app/docs/ed-errata.txt:79-84, environment/app/docs/ed.txt:942-947, solution/pyed/ed.py:689-723, solution/pyed/ed.py:740-754
    3. (Major) [1] A backslash-continued global list stops consuming input at its empty continuation line, so a following q executes after all selected lines instead of as part of the list.
       Reach: Start with an existing two-line file containing `x\ny\n` and supply `g/./\\\n\nq\n` on standard input. The errata explicitly says the empty segment prints each selected line twice and the following q belongs to the list. Thus q stops list execution during the first selected line: the expected printed lines are `x\nx\n`. The reference assembles only the first two script lines into the list, printing `x\nx\ny\ny\n`, then reads q as a top-level command. Flip: stdout has two extra `y` lines, contrary to the required byte-for-byte comparison.

## Pre-Difficulty Gate Failed

Difficulty not run: the submission did not pass every blocking quality or quality panel check. Oracle/NOP already passed. No Opus, GPT, analysis, or rubric-generation runs were started.

QUALITY PANEL: NEEDS REVISION -- 28 blocking issues to fix. Details for each are below.

Blocking (fix every one):
   1. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: No option case checks that -p consumes a hyphen-leading next
      argument as its prompt string.  (confirmed by running the grader)
   2. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: The corpus never applies the list command to a line long enough to
      exercise GNU ed's list-output wrapping.  (confirmed by running the grader)
   3. [Correct Reference Solution] MAJOR: The bracket parser interprets a hyphen in the first
      position as the lower endpoint of a range instead of a literal character.
   4. [Correct Reference Solution] MAJOR: A substitution with no match returns success inside a
      global command list, bypassing the global list's first-error stop.
   5. [Correct Reference Solution] MAJOR: The reference does not accept GNU ed's documented long
      option spellings, including the in-scope --prompt=STRING form, because its parser only
      recognizes individual characters after one leading hyphen.
   6. [Correct Reference Solution] MAJOR: Unset apostrophe marks resolve to address 0 even after
      the buffer becomes nonempty, contrary to GNU ed 1.19's explicitly documented erratum.
   7. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: The corpus never exercises a line near the permitted 100000-byte
      length, so a plausible 81920-byte input cap passes.
   8. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: No case joins a still-remembered unterminated line as the last
      component, so a join that incorrectly retains that line's missing newline passes.
   9. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: The corpus never reads an unterminated NUL-free file into an
      already-text buffer, leaving that newline-appending branch unchecked.
  10. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: No case checks the exceptional added-newline byte count when a
      read into the middle of a text buffer itself makes that buffer binary.
  11. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: The corpus tests addresses on quit commands but does not
      distinguish an implementation that accepts an address on undo.
  12. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: No case requires a valid basic bounded repeat whose lower bound is
      zero.
  13. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: Combined suffix tests cover several ordinary commands but never
      require an input-mode command to honor its print suffix.
  14. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: FILE-parameter separator cases use spaces, leaving the documented
      whitespace separator untested for tabs.
  15. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: No graded case checks that joining a marked line invalidates its
      mark.
  16. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: The `l` cases never require escaping a literal backslash, allowing
      an otherwise correct list formatter to print that character unchanged.
  17. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: The omitted-final-delimiter cases do not test that a substitution
      affecting multiple lines prints the last affected line.
  18. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: No case rejects an ordinary substitution suffix that is forbidden
      on the abbreviated repeat form.
  19. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: The corpus does not exercise the contract-permitted 100,000-byte
      line boundary, instead topping out at a 70,000-byte fixture.
  20. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: No case supplies EOF while a matching interactive G or V command
      is waiting for its command list, despite the contract assigning that situation an error
      disposition.
  21. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: No graded case verifies that -s suppresses the byte count produced
      by the uppercase E edit command.
  22. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: The corpus never distinguishes an implementation of \b that
      recognizes only word beginnings from one that recognizes both word beginnings and endings.
  23. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: The corpus does not verify that \w includes digits or that \W
      accepts non-whitespace punctuation.
  24. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: No case verifies that c copies every line of a deleted range,
      rather than only one line, into the cut buffer.
  25. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: The verifier never observes the cut buffer immediately after d, so
      an implementation may omit d's cut-buffer update.
  26. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: The verifier never makes GNU ed's specified initial z window size
      (22 when no screen size is known) observable, so an incorrect initial default passes every
      case.
  27. [Sound Verifier] MAJOR: The largest tested input line is 70,000 bytes, leaving the
      documented 70,001-100,000-byte portion of the task input range untested.
  28. [Sound Verifier] MINOR: The process and native-code guard can be disabled by the candidate

3. [Correct Reference Solution] MAJOR -- Core domain and business logic

   instead of a literal character.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: Supply pipe stdin `a\na\n0\n.\ng/[-a]/p\nQ\n`. The manual requires the first `-` in

6. [Correct Reference Solution] MAJOR -- core domain and business logic
   Unset apostrophe marks resolve to address 0 even after the buffer becomes nonempty, contrary
   to GNU ed 1.19's explicitly documented erratum.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: run with stdin as a pipe: `a\nx\n.\n'a=\nQ\n`. After `a`, the buffer has one line.
     On `'a=`, get_marked_node_addr reads marks[0], which is None, and calls
     get_line_node_addr(None). That walk advances from head through the sole line back to head,
     then returns 0 because its invalid-address test is guarded by `if addr`; it therefore does
     not fail. The `=` command emits `0\n`. GNU ed must reject this unset mark once a line
     exists, emitting `?\n`; without -l it also records an error and exits nonzero, whereas this
     reference exits 0 after Q. Flip: stdout is `0\n` rather than `?\n`, and the exit status
     differs. The contract's errata expressly distinguishes the empty-buffer case from the
     nonempty case.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/ed-errata.txt:10-14, solution/pyed/ed.py:168-179,
     solution/pyed/ed.py:922-927, solution/pyed/ed.py:1329-1333

fields.label: Quality Judge Panel Feedback
fields.description:
After initial submission, you will be provided with detailed feedback along 5 axes, each answering a core question about your task:

  1. Coherent Contracts: Can a candidate determine every rule used to grade the task?
  2. Correct Reference Solution: Does the reference satisfy the documented task?
  3. Protected Ground Truth: Can candidate code obtain or control the answer the grader trusts?
  4. Sound Verifier: Does grading reject wrong solutions and accept contract-valid ones?
  5. Deterministic Execution: Does the same submission receive stable grading on repeated runs?

Keep these in mind when reviewing this feedback, and refer to the guidelines for more details on this feedback.
